description: Elizabeth continues her vigil at Netherfield, facing the barely concealed disdain of the Bingley sisters. A spirited debate on the nature of 'accomplished women' reveals the deep intellectual and moral divide between Elizabeth, the Bingleys, and Mr. Darcy.

analysis_entries.anchor: Elizabeth to the enjoyment of all her original dislike.
analysis_entries.note: Elizabeth's 'enjoyment' of her dislike highlights her spirited, if somewhat prejudiced, character. She finds psychological comfort in her low opinion of the Bingley sisters, which contrasts with Bingley's genuine concern for Jane.

analysis_entries.anchor: mixture of pride and impertinence: she had no conversation
analysis_entries.note: The Bingley sisters' critique of Elizabeth reveals more about their own social rigidity than Elizabeth's shortcomings. They define 'style' and 'taste' through a lens of class superiority, dismissing her authentic vitality as 'impertinence.'

analysis_entries.anchor: six inches deep in mud, I am absolutely certain
analysis_entries.note: The obsession with Elizabeth’s muddy petticoat serves as a powerful symbol of the divide between those who prioritize social decorum and those who prioritize family duty and physical action.

analysis_entries.anchor: show an abominable sort of conceited independence, a most
analysis_entries.note: Miss Bingley's use of the word 'independence' as an insult is central to the novel's themes. To the Bingleys, independence is 'conceited,' whereas to Elizabeth, it is a necessary part of her integrity.

analysis_entries.anchor: they repaired to her room on leaving the dining-parlour
analysis_entries.note: The 'renewal of tenderness' shown by the sisters is performed only when it is socially required, illustrating the performative nature of their empathy compared to Elizabeth’s genuine devotion.

Darcy's pride in Pemberley’s library as the 'work of many generations' underscores his deep connection to his lineage and tradition, suggesting that his character is built on a foundation more substantial than the Bingleys' new wealth.

analysis_entries.anchor: add something more substantial in the improvement of her mind
analysis_entries.note: Darcy’s addition to the list of 'accomplishments'—the improvement of the mind through reading—elevates the standard from mere social performance to intellectual substance, signaling his intellectual alignment with Elizabeth.

quote_entries.anchor: Elizabeth was so much caught by what passed
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="The Internal Observer">“Elizabeth was so much caught by what passed, as to leave her very little attention for her book.”</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: Why must _she_ be scampering about the country
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="The Scandal of Sincerity">“Why must _she_ be scampering about the country, because her sister had a cold? Her hair so untidy, so blowzy!”</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: It shows an affection for her sister that is very pleasing
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Bingley’s Kindness">“It shows an affection for her sister that is very pleasing,” said Bingley.</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: they were brightened by the exercise.
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Darcy’s Admiration">“Not at all,” he replied: “they were brightened by the exercise.”</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: I deserve neither such praise nor such censure
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Elizabeth’s Self-Knowledge">“I deserve neither such praise nor such censure,” cried Elizabeth; “I am _not_ a great reader, and I have pleasure in many things.”</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: I rather wonder now at your knowing _any_.
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="The High Bar of Accomplishment">“I am no longer surprised at your knowing _only_ six accomplished women. I rather wonder now at your knowing _any_.”</Callout>

quote_entries.anchor: Whatever bears affinity to cunning is despicable.
quote_entries.callout: <Callout variant="quote" title="Darcy’s Moral Compass">“Undoubtedly,” replied Darcy... “Whatever bears affinity to cunning is despicable.”</Callout>
